lines.text: On April 11th, 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on what was intended to be humanity's third landing on the lunar surface.
lines.spoken: On April 11th, 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on what was intended to be humanity's third landing on the lunar surface.

lines.text: Commanded by veteran astronaut Jim Lovell alongside command module pilot Jack Swigert and lunar module pilot Fred Haise, the mission began without incident.
lines.spoken: Commanded by veteran astronaut Jim Lovell alongside command module pilot Jack Swigert and lunar module pilot Fred Haise, the mission began without incident.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; CREW • LOVELL, SWIGERT, HAISE

lines.text: Two days later, on the evening of April 13th, the spacecraft was coasting smoothly two hundred thousand miles from Earth.
lines.spoken: Two days later, on the evening of April 13th, the spacecraft was coasting smoothly two hundred thousand miles from Earth.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; APRIL 13 • 200,000 MILES OUT

lines.text: At 55 hours and 54 minutes into the flight, mission controller Sy Liebergot noticed low pressure in a hydrogen tank and asked the crew to stir their cryogenic tanks.
lines.spoken: At 55 hours and 54 minutes into the flight, mission controller Sy Liebergot noticed low pressure in a hydrogen tank and asked the crew to stir their cryogenic tanks.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; ROUTINE CRYOGENIC STIR

lines.text: Jack Swigert reached up to the main panel and flipped the fan switches in Oxygen Tank Number Two.
lines.spoken: Jack Swigert reached up to the main panel and flipped the fan switches in Oxygen Tank Number Two.

lines.text: Deep inside the tank, teflon-insulated wiring that had been subtly damaged during pre-flight testing produced a sudden electrical spark in pure liquid oxygen.
lines.spoken: Deep inside the tank, teflon-insulated wiring that had been subtly damaged during pre-flight testing produced a sudden electrical spark in pure liquid oxygen.

lines.text: A violent pressure pulse blew off an outer access door. An explosion ripped through the side of the Service Module into the vacuum of space.
lines.spoken: A violent pressure pulse blew off an outer access door. An explosion ripped through the side of the Service Module into the vacuum of space.

lines.text: Moments later, Jack Swigert radioed back to Houston the historic words: 'Houston, we've had a problem here.'
lines.spoken: Moments later, Jack Swigert radioed back to Houston the historic words: 'Houston, we've had a problem here.'
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; HOUSTON, WE'VE HAD A PROBLEM

lines.text: Looking out of the hatch window, Jim Lovell confirmed the nightmare: a gas was actively venting in high volume from the side of their spacecraft.
lines.spoken: Looking out of the hatch window, Jim Lovell confirmed the nightmare: a gas was actively venting in high volume from the side of their spacecraft.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; VENTING INTO THE VOID

lines.text: Oxygen Tank 2 was completely destroyed, and Tank 1 was rapidly leaking down to zero. The Command Module Odyssey was losing all electrical power and dying.
lines.spoken: Oxygen Tank 2 was completely destroyed, and Tank 1 was rapidly leaking down to zero. The Command Module Odyssey was losing all electrical power and dying.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; COMMAND MODULE FAILING

lines.text: Lead flight director Gene Kranz and his team realized the Moon landing was impossible. The only priority was keeping three men alive.
lines.spoken: Lead flight director Gene Kranz and his team realized the Moon landing was impossible. The only priority was keeping three men alive.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; GENE KRANZ • FAILURE IS NOT AN OPTION
lines.typed: GENE KRANZ • FAILURE IS NOT AN OPTION

lines.text: The crew had minutes to power up the Lunar Module Aquarius, transforming a craft designed for two men for two days into a life raft for three.
lines.spoken: The crew had minutes to power up the Lunar Module Aquarius, transforming a craft designed for two men for two days into a life raft for three.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; AQUARIUS • THE LIFE RAFT

lines.text: To conserve power for atmospheric reentry, Odyssey was completely shut down. The temperature inside Aquarius plummeted to three degrees Celsius.
lines.spoken: To conserve power for atmospheric reentry, Odyssey was completely shut down. The temperature inside Aquarius plummeted to three degrees Celsius.

lines.text: Carbon dioxide levels rose to lethal thresholds, forcing engineers on Earth to invent an adapter using cardboard flight manuals, plastic bags, and duct tape.
lines.spoken: Carbon dioxide levels rose to lethal thresholds, forcing engineers on Earth to invent an adapter using cardboard flight manuals, plastic bags, and duct tape.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; DUCT TAPE & CARDBOARD

lines.text: A critical engine burn around the far side of the moon slingshot Apollo 13 onto a free-return trajectory back toward Earth.
lines.spoken: A critical engine burn around the far side of the moon slingshot Apollo 13 onto a free-return trajectory back toward Earth.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; FREE RETURN TRAJECTORY

lines.text: Four days of bone-chilling cold, dehydration, and razor-thin mathematical calculations culminated in a flawless reentry into the Pacific Ocean.
lines.spoken: Four days of bone-chilling cold, dehydration, and razor-thin mathematical calculations culminated in a flawless reentry into the Pacific Ocean.
lines.hero: archival photograph lands; APRIL 17 • PACIFIC REENTRY

lines.text: What should have been NASA's greatest disaster became humanity's most extraordinary triumph of engineering and human will.
lines.spoken: What should have been NASA's greatest disaster became humanity's most extraordinary triumph of engineering and human will.
